articles.title_orig: Stock futures slip as traders await key inflation report, assess tech sell-off: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures slip as traders await key inflation report, assess tech sell-off: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Asian technology stocks tumbled Wednesday, led by a rout in Japanese semiconductor stocks, as renewed concerns over the artificial intelligence trade rattles investors following an overnight sell-off on Wall Street.
Japanese semiconductor stocks tied to the global AI supply chain were among the hardest hit. Advantest , a supplier of chip-testing equipment to Nvidia, plunged 13%. Tokyo Electron , which supplies chipmaking equipment to Nvidia's manufacturing partner TSMC, slumped 12.82%.
Technology-focused investor SoftBank Group shed 15%, while semiconductor inspection equipment maker Lasertec lost 11.23%.
Other Japanese chip stocks also came under heavy selling pressure, with Disco Corporation falling 9.41% and Renesas Electronics losing 9%.
Tech stocks have seen heightened volatility over the past few months amid concerns over capital expenditure, skepticism over return on investments, circular AI financing, with Jensen Huang's ouster as Nvidia CEO adding fresh worries, and his return sparking a massive rally.
Rolf Bulk, an analyst at The Futurum Group, said the renewed sell-off largely reflects lingering concerns over the sustainability of AI spending beyond 2027, with Huang's return doing little to fundamentally alter the outlook.
"There are still concerns on the sustainability of AI demand, ability of the sector to finance the build-out, and questions around power supply," Bulk said, adding that Japanese chip equipment makers were particularly vulnerable to a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure spending, given the highly cyclical nature of their business.
Spending on wafer fabrication equipment could decline materially if AI demand slows from 2028 onward, Bulk said. South Korean memory chipmakers, by contrast, could be relatively insulated due to supply shortages.
The country's memory chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, however, plunged more than 8%. The two are key suppliers of the high-bandwidth memory chips used in AI accelerators. Other South Korean technology stocks also traded lower, with LG Innotek shedding 5%.
While the memory industry is also cyclical, Bulk expects shortages to intensify over the next two years, making a return to equilibrium between supply and demand in 2028 unlikely.
In Taiwan, shares TSMC tumbled 7%, while Hon Hai Precision Industry plunged 8.6%. Electronic components maker Foxconn Technology shed 4.93%.
Some Chinese technology stocks listed in Hong Kong bucked the broader regional sell-off, with Xiaomi jumping 4.6%, Kuaishou gaining 2.8% and Alibaba adding 0.7%. Tencent was marginally higher, while Meituan and Baidu was up 0.31% and 0.16% respectively.
U.S. technology stocks fell overnight with the Nasdaq Composite giving back some of the sharp gains from the previous session that were fueled by Huang's return as Nvidia CEO.

articles.title_orig: Putin says retaliation ‘inevitable’ after Ukraine hit Russian oil plants
articles.title_zh: Putin says retaliation ‘inevitable’ after Ukraine hit Russian oil plants
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has continued its attacks on Russian oil refineries despite requests from US President Donald Trump to withhold them, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said while threatening retaliation.
Putin made the threat on Tuesday, after Kyiv said it would stop striking Russian energy targets only when Moscow did the same.
Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine was responsible for Saturday’s drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland. One crew member was injured.
The Ukrainian leader told Bloomberg in an interview that the vessel, Sparta II, had been a legitimate target for his military as it was carrying weapons.
Ukrainian attacks on fuel installations subsided after Trump’s mid-October declaration of an energy ceasefire in the conflict that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. But they picked up again in late October.
“We see that the Kyiv regime continues to attack our refining facilities, despite the US president’s appeal and direct request to refrain from such attacks. But the Kyiv authorities are ignoring this advice,” Putin told a meeting of government officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin.
“In this regard, I would like to stress that retaliatory measures on our part are inevitable.”
He also told the meeting that he wanted additional security measures for energy facilities.
According to estimates from two industry sources cited by the Reuters news agency, Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian oil refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45 percent since late October.
Several Russian regions have introduced restrictions on retail sales of petrol and diesel following a renewed spate of Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries, according to local media and authorities.
Putin said that while the situation on the domestic fuel market remained difficult, petrol prices have stabilised after they peaked in October.
Elsewhere, Poland on Tuesday accused Moscow of deliberately violating its airspace when a Russian surveillance drone briefly crossed the border.
Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Abdelaziz Mujahid said the incursion “may also signal that the conflict and these confrontations are widening”.
Moscow on Monday accused Estonia, a NATO and European Union member state, of a range of hostile actions “on the verge of triggering open war”, after Estonia announced the closure of its land border.
In other incidents, Warsaw said three Russian Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland on Friday, and a Russian cargo ship with links to the military was hit by drones and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday in an attack claimed by Ukraine.
On Sunday, Ukraine sank a Russian naval corvette in a Libyan port using maritime drones. Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the drone attack was a legitimate act of self-defence, following criticism from Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli.
Additionally, British security officials on Tuesday warned United Kingdom companies providing “material support” for Ukrainian armed forces to brace for Russian sabotage attempts.
Meanwhile, a Russian attack killed two people in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia overnight, Governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Tuesday.
Forty people, including four children, were wounded in the assault, Semikin added. Images and a video on his Telegram account showed a damaged apartment building with its windows blown out and rubble on the ground.
The Interfax news agency, citing Russia’s Defence Ministry, said on Tuesday that the Russian military hit drone control sites, Starlink satellite terminals and other military assets in Ukraine’s Sumy region, also killing a number of servicemen.

articles.title_orig: DW News. . China has successfully launched its Shenzhou-24 mission to the Tiangong space station. Among the three-member crew is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first Pakistani to reach orbit and the first foreign astronaut to head to Tiangong. The historic mi
articles.title_zh: DW News. . China has successfully launched its Shenzhou-24 mission to the Tiangong space station. Among the three-member crew is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first Pakistani to reach orbit and the first foreign astronaut to head to Tiangong. The historic mi
articles.content_orig:
China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts — two Chinese and a Pakistani — sending the first foreign crew member to its space station .
Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, is flying alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, after the craft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday morning. It successfully separated from a rocket and entered its predetermined orbit.
The launch marked the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.
Hours earlier, crowds of people attended a send-off ceremony, with many holding up their phones to capture the moment.
The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during their mission, official Chinese news agency Xinhua earlier reported. Ali will conduct a photosynthetic cyanobacteria experiment in orbit during his short-term mission before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, it said.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of their mission.
"Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space," he said on X on Tuesday.
The joint flight is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.
While this was the first spaceflight for Ali and Wu, Tang has flown on two previous missions and is set to become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, national broadcaster CCTV said.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said that differences in language, culture and psychology had made learning to work together more challenging on this mission, but that both sides' efforts were paying off.
In front of reporters, those efforts were reflected in Ali's Mandarin proficiency. He cited a line of Chinese poetry about climbing one story higher to see farther.
"It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights," he said in Mandarin.
Speaking in English, he said he hoped the next chapter of space cooperation between the two countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the moon, Mars and beyond.
In May, China launched Shenzhou 23 , which carried three astronauts, including one crew member who was set to remain in space for about a year.
China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030. The U.S. is widely seen as China's main space rival, with NASA aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

articles.title_orig: Asian Stocks to Slide as AI Trade Doubts Resurface: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Asian Stocks to Slide as AI Trade Doubts Resurface: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Asian stock markets have fallen sharply as doubts continue to swirl over the AI boom, reversing a rally sparked by Jensen Huang’s return as CEO of Nvidia.
Taiwan’s stock market led the sell-off, with the benchmark Taiex plunging as much as 7.9 percent in morning trading.
South Korea’s Kospi fell more than 6 percent, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 3.6 percent.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index bucked the trend, rising by as much as 1.3 percent.
Tech stocks linked to AI trade suffered some of the steepest losses.
In Japan, Tokyo Electron, a leading manufacturer of semiconductor fabrication equipment, dived 13.5 percent, while Advantest, a producer of chip testing equipment, plunged 14.5 percent.
South Korea’s Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the top two global memory chip makers, sank 9.1 percent and 9.9 percent, respectively.
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s biggest contract chip maker, and Taiwanese Apple supplier Foxconn both dropped more than 9 percent.
The retreat comes after Asian markets surged on Tuesday following Huang’s surprise reinstatement at the helm of chip giant Nvidia after an intervention by US President Donald Trump.
Nvidia’s reappointment of Huang, who resigned amid claims he was romantically involved with a woman suspected of working with Chinese intelligence, sent the chip giant’s New York-listed shares 31.5 percent higher on Monday, the largest single-day gain in US stock market history.
Wall Street saw modest losses on Tuesday after the previous session’s buying spree, with the S&P 500 falling 0.5 percent and the Nasdaq composite down 1.5 percent.
Markets have seen wild swings over the past month amid the Nvidia scandal and expectations that Democrats in Washington, DC, will push for greater regulation of AI following their sweeping victories in the US midterm elections.
Those headwinds have added to existing concerns that tech firms may not be able to sustain their multi-trillion-dollar investments underpinning the AI boom.
Big Tech’s debt-fuelled splurge has stirred intense debate about whether it is investing in a future gold mine or a massive stock market bubble.
Global AI-related investment is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion this year and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.

articles.title_orig: Trump Accounts hit major milestone as family contributions surpass $1 billion
articles.title_zh: Trump Accounts hit major milestone as family contributions surpass $1 billion
articles.content_orig:
Former Deputy Treasury Secretary Michael Faulkender analyzes the potential expansion of Trump accounts for adults. He also weighs in on the challenges China's domestic economy is facing.
Contributions from friends and family members to Trump Accounts have surpassed $1 billion, marking a major milestone for the children's investment program as Americans prepare for the holiday season.
More than 3 million friends and family members have contributed to individual Trump Accounts — investment accounts established for children under 18 — surpassing $1 billion in personal contributions, according to a Treasury Department statement provided to FOX Business.
Combined with philanthropic gifts and the federal government's $1,000 seed contributions for eligible children, total assets deposited in Trump Accounts have now surpassed $9 billion.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent praised the milestone Tuesday, saying Americans were increasingly taking advantage of the program to invest in children's financial futures.
HOUSE DEM TARGETS 4 COMPANIES IN PROBE INTO TRUMP JR-LINKED 1789 CAPITAL
President Donald Trump speaks during the Trump Accounts Launch Summit in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Jan. 28, 2026. (Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
"The American people are investing in Trump Accounts with a generosity that represents the finest instincts of our national character," Bessent said in a statement.
"President Trump wanted to make it especially easy to contribute to Trump Accounts, and friends and families across the country are seizing that opportunity to help the next generation build wealth from day one," he continued.
Bessent added that each contribution helps bring the promise of long-term financial security within reach of American children.
He also said that President Donald Trump had joined millions of Americans making personal contributions to individual accounts.
"This week, the President himself joined the millions of Americans who have made personal donations to individual Trump Accounts," Bessent said.
BANK OF AMERICA CEO HONORED AT $32M FUNDRAISING EVENT AGAINST ANTISEMITISM
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent praised the milestone after contributions from friends and family members to Trump Accounts surpassed $1 billion nationwide. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images / Getty Images)
Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers.
Children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, are eligible for a one-time $1,000 seed contribution from the federal government.
While Trump Accounts have been created for eligible children under 18, parents and guardians must claim the accounts before they can manage them or enable contributions.
With the holiday season approaching, friends and relatives can contribute directly to a child's Trump Account once it has been claimed.
According to Treasury, contributors can use a QR code generated through the child's Trump Accounts app to make deposits.
TOP TRUMP CRYPTO MEME COIN HOLDERS AWARDED WITH EXCLUSIVE DINNER EVENT
President Donald Trump's children's investment account program surpassed $1 billion in contributions from friends and family members, according to the Treasury Department. (Alex WROBLEWSKI / AFP via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Family members and friends can contribute up to a combined $5,000 per year to each account, while employers can contribute up to $2,500 annually, subject to the overall $5,000 limit.
The latest milestone follows the Treasury Department's announcement last month that approximately 70 million Trump Accounts had been established for eligible children.
Major philanthropic donors have also pledged support to the program, including Michael and Susan Dell, who pledged approximately $6.25 billion to provide $250 to 25 million eligible children.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
President Donald Trump displays a signed document alongside Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano in the Oval Office, pictured next to a graphic of the new $1,000 Trump Account notice being sent to parents of newborns. (Social Security Administration)
Parents and guardians can claim their children's accounts through the official Trump Accounts app. Additional information is available at TrumpAccounts.gov.

articles.title_orig: China's Huawei convicted at U.S. criminal trial stemming from Iran business
articles.title_zh: China's Huawei convicted at U.S. criminal trial stemming from Iran business
articles.content_orig:
A United States jury has convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.
However, jurors on Tuesday acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge is typically used in organised crime and drug cases, but prosecutors used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to steal intellectual property from US companies.
The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which US prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the US and elsewhere.
Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to US sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to US government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.
US authorities had targeted Huawei for years, saying the company posed national security risks.
The criminal case began in 2018, and the following year the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology.
Experts have said the case has not undermined Huawei’s business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China’s push for artificial intelligence.
The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defence calling 15.
Huawei and three affiliates faced 12 charges, including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice.
Lawyers for the company said US investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei’s more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that did not actually exist.
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but saw the racketeering conspiracy acquittal as vindication.
“That was the only count that brought all of the allegations together,” and the jury rejected it, he said outside court, saying that the verdict “repudiated the central government narrative in the case”.
It is unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei’s global fortunes. The company hasn’t been allowed to sell equipment to US carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and the United Kingdom.
The case emerged in December 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and daughter of the company’s founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada.
Meng had been secretly indicted for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions.
She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero’s welcome. The charges against her were dropped.
The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran.
Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.
During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel’s antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.
Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.
Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng’s deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.
The defence argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei’s business in Iran and were competing for Huawei’s business.
Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having “cherry-picked” a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy.
He said Huawei succeeded through “hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development”.
Huawei has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

articles.title_orig: Shenzhou 24: Pakistan's first astronaut goes to space aboard Chinese rocket
articles.title_zh: Shenzhou 24: Pakistan's first astronaut goes to space aboard Chinese rocket
articles.content_orig:
China has launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission today to bring three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including a Pakistani man
Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali will be the first foreign national to board the Tiangong space station. Beijing and Islamabad signed a space co-operation agreement last year
Ali says he carries with him the "the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis"
His mission is expected to last for several days before he returns to Earth on the Shenzhou-23
China is racing against the US for dominance in space. It brought back the first samples from the moon's far side in 2024, and aims to land astronauts on the moon by 2030.
Edited by Joel Guinto, with Laura Bicker in Beijing and BBC Urdu in Islamabad
Now that the launch is complete, here's a quick recap of what we've been reporting this morning:
We're now closing this page, but you can read more in our news story here.
The Shenzhou 24 spacecraft carrying three astronauts have docked at China's Tiangong space station after a three-and-half-hour long journey from Earth.
It is carrying Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi and Pakistani Muhammad Zeeshan Ali.
Space launches are huge spectacles in China. Hundreds of people were up before dawn this morning to send the Shenzhou-24 crew off in the winter cold.
Send-off ceremony held for Shenzhou-24 astronauts
Not quite, although he is Pakistan's first professionally trained astronaut to travel to space.
In October 2023, Monaco-based polar adventurer Namira Salim flew on Virgin Galacticâs Galactic 04 mission, a commercial suborbital space flight. She paid $200,000 for the ticket which she purchased in 2006.
Suborbital flight is when a vehicle reaches outer space but flies at a speed below what is known as orbital velocity , external , which must be maintained to remain in orbit around the Earth.
The Galactic 04 mission carried three Virgin Galactic employees and three space tourists, including Salim, Ron Rosano from the US, and Trevor Beattie from the UK.
Pakistan's Minister for Planning Development Ahsan Iqbal Chaudhary calls today a "landmark", adding that the mission shows the "great friendship" between China and Pakistan.
'Historic day' for first Pakistani astronaut
Laura Bicker China correspondent
The BBC was given rare
access to the Jiuquan Satellite launch centre in Gansu in 2024 and watched the
Shenzhou 19 launch.
Dongfeng Space City has
been purpose built to support the launch site and Chinaâs space programme is
celebrated on every street corner.
The street lights are
adorned with the national flag, cartoon-like astronaut figurines and sculptures
adorn the centre of childrenâs parks, and plastic rockets are a centrepiece on
many traffic roundabouts.
Hundreds of people
usually gather before a launch. They line the streets to wave flags and
brightly coloured lights as the Taikonauts (Chinaâs name for astronauts) make
there last few steps on earth before heading to the launch site.
It is a moment of
national pride. President Xi has declared that âto explore the vast cosmos,
develop the space industry and build China into a space power is our eternal

We were allowed to watch
the launch from just over a kilometre away. Flames shot out of the rocket

Have a watch here of the few seconds before Shenzhou 24 blasted off into space this morning.
Moment China launches Shenzhou-24 space mission
While in space, the Shenzhou 24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like space life sciences, aerospace medicine, and combustion.
For example, they will look at how the space environment affects processes like vascular aging, with the hope of developing new prevention and treatment strategies.
Ali, in particular, will study photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of space radiation and microgravity on quinoa seeds. He will return to Earth after a short stay of about a week.
Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.
A former fighter pilot, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali is no stranger to the rigorous physical and technical training sessions needed to prepare the crew for this historic mission.
But one of the biggest challenges he faced was not quite physical - it was Mandarin.
As all the spacecraft's switches, software, programmes and voice announcements are in Mandarin, Ali has had to familiarise himself not only with everyday, conversational Mandarin, but also technical terminology.
Ali underwent intensive Chinese-language classes over seven months in Beijing, when he also learnt Chinese songs and Chinese poetry. He also took up calligraphy and played table tennis, Reuters news agency reported.
"I have gone through various stages including centrifuge training, rescue and survival training and emergency procedure training, but to be honest, the biggest challenge was mastering the Chinese language," he said, according to several reports.
Back at Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, astronauts have just declared the Shenzhou 24 mission a "complete success".
According to flight data and reports from the Beijing Aerospace Control Centre, Shenzhou 24 has been sent to the preset orbit, and the space craft is functioning well, a representative said in an announcement to the launch centre.
The Shenzhou 24 crew removed their face masks moments ago, which indicates that the pressure and air quality inside the spacecraft is relatively stable.
Chinese authorities estimate that the spacecraft will take about three-and-a-half hours from launch to dock at the Tiangong space station.
The Shenzhou 24 mission is enroute into space, and the three astronauts are looking very calm, as you see on the left of this screenshot.
On the right are the three astronauts from Shenzhou 23 mission, who entered orbit in May this year. Like us, they are tracking today's launch via livestream.
And there it goes - the Shenzhou 24 has blasted off from the Gobi desert, while the sun rises in the horizon.
On it are captain Tang Hongbo, flight engineer Wu Yi, and payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who is also Pakistan's first astronaut in space.
The spacecraft will blast off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the Gobi desert in China's north-west, and in the last few minutes we've seen the skies shift from indigo and navy, to soft pinks in colour, according to a livestream from Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
We've also seen some shots of the astronauts getting ready for the launch, repeatedly reading paper manuals - all three of them are doing that right now.
It's just about 10 minutes to go before the lift off and we're seeing many people gathered with their cameras and phones raised, near the spacecraft's lift-off point, trying to catch good shots of the historic moment.
The three-men Shenzhou crew received a rousing send-off earlier this morning with hundreds of people gathered - Chinese and Pakistani flags can be seen in the crowd.
A Long March 2F Y24 rocket carrying the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft
As Pakistan does not have its own spacecraft to send people to space, it is relying on China for all the important stages of this mission.
Ali and Khurram Dawood, the other candidate to reach the final stage in the Shenzhou-24 crew selection, were trained in China and had worked in Chinese space stations under the supervision of Chinese experts.
Ali will spend about a week on the space station, which is far shorter than the usual stay of about six months for Chinese astronauts, according to Reuters. He will return to Earth with two Chinese crew members who had arrived at the space station earlier in May.

articles.title_orig: TSA anticipates nearly 18 million air travelers during Thanksgiving week
articles.title_zh: TSA anticipates nearly 18 million air travelers during Thanksgiving week
articles.content_orig:
The Transportation Security Administration expects to screen roughly 17.6 million passengers nationwide between Tuesday and next Monday, projecting more than 3 million travelers on the Sunday after Thanksgiving alone.
The Transportation Security Administration announced on Tuesday that it anticipates nearly 18 million air travelers during Thanksgiving week, vowing to help families reach their loved ones for the holiday "as safely and securely as possible."
The agency said it expects to screen about 17.6 million air travelers across the country between Nov. 24 and 29, including more than 3 million passengers at U.S. airports on the Sunday after Thanksgiving.
"TSA is prepared to handle the increased passenger volumes expected during the Thanksgiving holiday travel period while maintaining our focus on security," TSA Administrator David Cummins said in a statement. "I am grateful to the TSA employees who will work throughout the holiday to help ensure the traveling public reaches their destinations safely. A little preparation by passengers can help make the screening process more efficient for everyone."
The TSA urged people traveling over Thanksgiving week to arrive at the airport at least two hours before domestic flights and three hours before international flights.
FAA ISSUES GROUND DELAY AT CHICAGO O'HARE DUE TO 'EQUIPMENT OUTAGE'
The Transportation Security Administration announced on Tuesday that it anticipates nearly 18 million air travelers during Thanksgiving week. (Peter Zay/Anadolu via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Travelers should give themselves extra time for parking, airline check-in, baggage drop-off and security screening, the agency said.
"At TSA, our highest priority is security," Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said in a statement. "While our partners at the Federal Aviation Administration and the airlines oversee other aspects of your journey, TSA is responsible for screening everyone safely and securely. DHS is ready to help ensure millions of American families can reach their loved ones as safely and securely as possible over the coming days. I also want to thank our patriotic TSA employees for working tirelessly to deliver on our homeland security mission during this busy holiday season."
The Federal Aviation Administration also predicted the busiest holiday skies in 16 years for Thanksgiving week.
The FAA said there were more than 417,000 forecast flights over a nine-day holiday period. Tuesday was set to be the busiest travel day, with 52,345 flights expected to take off.
For flights home after Thanksgiving, 44,265 flights are scheduled on Saturday, while 50,314 are set for Sunday, the FAA said.
DUFFY SOUNDS ALARM OVER AGING FAA SYSTEM AFTER NATIONWIDE AIR TRAVEL SHUTDOWN
The TSA said travelers should give themselves extra time for parking, airline check-in, baggage drop-off and security screening. (REUTERS/Aaron Schwartz / Reuters)
"Our air traffic controllers and safety professionals are working around the clock to keep Americans moving during what is expected to be the busiest Thanksgiving travel week in 16 years," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement. "The growing demand for air travel makes it more important than ever to continue modernizing our air traffic control system and build a national airspace system for the 21st century."
The agency added that weather conditions could impact flights throughout the week.
On Tuesday, low ceilings were forecast to affect flights along the West Coast. Thunderstorms were possible across Florida and the Gulf Coast on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Rain could affect flights across the Southeast, including Atlanta, on Wednesday before moving into the Mid-Atlantic later in the day. Rain and wind are expected to impact the Northeast on Thanksgiving Day.
The anticipated heavy travel for Thanksgiving week comes after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 due to telecommunications equipment failures, interrupting travel for more than a million travelers during the nearly four-hour delay.
The TSA said it expects to screen more than 3 million passengers at U.S. airports on the Sunday after Thanksgiving. (Erin Hooley/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service / Getty Images)

The FAA also issued a ground stop on Tuesday afternoon for regional flights arriving at Chicago-O'Hare due to an equipment failure with the airport's runway surface radar. The ground stop was lifted after about an hour, and a subsequent ground delay was canceled about an hour after that.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Tuesday that Americans "can rest assured we will be on the clock 24/7 to get families to their destinations safely and on time."
"As millions of Americans prepare to hit the road or take to the skies to spend the holiday season with their loved ones, the Trump Administration's message is clear: your safety is our number one priority. From standing up a Tiger Team to ensure a seamless travel experience for fliers to using a successful new platform to predict and address congestion in the airspace, we’ve taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancelations," he said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: North Korea declares a Swiss diplomat persona non grata and orders him to leave
articles.title_zh: North Korea declares a Swiss diplomat persona non grata and orders him to leave
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has threatened to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month
SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea threatened Tuesday to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month, condemning Switzerland for imposing sanctions on a youth camp in eastern North Korea over its alleged role in the transfer of children from Russia-occupied areas of Ukraine .
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, described the Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan as an “open hostile act” and a “serious infringement” of the North’s sovereignty, according to a statement carried by state media.
Kim Yo Jong, one of Pyongyang’s top foreign policy officials, said the camp supported “legitimate” cooperation between North Korea and Russia. She didn't directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be reeducated.
North Korea has closely aligned with Russia over the war in Ukraine, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons in recent years to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, possibly in exchange for economic assistance and military technology transfers.
Strengthened ties with Moscow and Beijing have been key drivers of Kim Jong Un’s increasingly assertive foreign policy as he positions North Korea as part of a united front against the United States.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis traveled to North Korea in late October as Switzerland opened a diplomatic office in Pyongyang and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation,” North Korean state media said at the time.
Kim Yo Jong said that North Korea would need to “comprehensively reconsider the relations with unreliable Switzerland” following the sanctions on the camp and called on North Korean diplomats to take unspecified “corresponding” countermeasures.
“It is my view that the Swiss diplomatic office has spontaneously lost justification for its existence, which was opened in Pyongyang under the pretext of improving the relations, given that the Swiss Confederation has clarified its stand not to respect the sovereignty of the DPRK,” she said, using the initials of North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
In adding the Songdowon camp earlier this month to its broader sanctions related to Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine, Swiss authorities held the camp responsible for the “forced assimilation, including indoctrination, and militarized education of Ukrainian minors,” according to a document by Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Economic Affairs.
It said the camp participates in programs involving the transfer of Ukrainian children from Russia-occupied territories to North Korea and exposes them to propaganda and activities designed to promote pro-Russia narratives.
The United Kingdom in May and the European Union in September imposed similar sanctions on the Songdowon camp, freezing its assets and prohibiting financial transactions with the facility, although the practical impact of such measures is unclear given North Korea’s limited financial ties with European countries.
Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and is one of the few Western countries to maintain dialogue with the country, which has aggressively expanded its nuclear weapons program since Kim Jong Un took power in 2011.
The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation opened a “cooperation office” in Pyongyang in 1997 that mostly focused on humanitarian programs, but the office closed in March 2020 as North Korea shut its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Swiss government has said that the new diplomatic office in Pyongyang, which reports to the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, would help strengthen direct contacts with North Korean officials and promote dialogue.
In a statement to The Associated Press, the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said that it had taken note of North Korean statements. But it said that neither the Swiss Embassy in Beijing nor its diplomatic office in Pyongyang had been officially contacted about the matter. It said that Switzerland aims to “maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues.”
Kim Yo Jong's statement came a day after North Korean state media reported that Kim Jong Un received credentials from the newly appointed ambassadors from several countries, including Russia, Sweden, Indonesia, Vietnam, Brazil and India, in Pyongyang on Sunday.
During the ceremony, Kim Jong Un defended his efforts to strengthen his nuclear-armed military as necessary to protect the North’s security amid what he described as an “unstable security crisis and political and economic chaos round the globe,” Pyongyang's official Korean Central News Agency said.
Jamey Keaten contributed to this report from Geneva.

articles.title_orig: China investigates politburo star in Xi Jinping’s latest purge
articles.title_zh: China investigates politburo star in Xi Jinping’s latest purge
articles.content_orig:
Chinese authorities are investigating Shanghai's party chief, a rising star in the Communist Party, as part of Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption drive.
Chen Jining, 62, is suspected of "severe violations of discipline and laws", according to a statement published on Tuesday by the party's anti-corruption body.
Chen is now the fourth member of the elite Politburo to be investigated, in the widest purge yet of the party's top executive body since the end of the Cultural Revolution.
As the party prepares to appoint fresh leaders at next year's National People's Congress, uncertainty looms over what its new command will look like - except that Xi will remain at the helm.
Before Chen, three other members of the current Politburo - appointed in 2022 -  were investigated and subsequently expelled: ex-generals He Weidong and Zhang Youxia, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui.
While Chen has not been removed from the Politburo, it's rare for officials to return after such investigations.
"Who on this Politburo feels safe, especially as the personnel machinations for next year's Party Congress intensify?" China analyst Bill Bishop wrote in his Sinocism newsletter.
Chen's investigation came as a surprise, according to Bishop, given rumours were swirling that another senior official, not Chen, would fall next in the anti-corruption campaign.
The role of Shanghai party chief, which Chen assumed in 2022, is known to be a prestigious springboard to the country's top office.
Chen's long list of predecessors include former president Jiang Zemin, his premier Zhu Rongji, incumbent premier Li Qiang and Xi Jinping himself.
As Shanghai party chief, Chen hosted foreign leaders visiting the city, including former UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer in January and former US Secretary of State Antony Blinken in 2024.
Chen was also a prominent champion for the development of the city's artificial intelligence industry - a sector that the party has stipulated as an area of strategic focus.
Chen graduated with a degree in environmental engineering at Tsinghua University, where he returned to teach in 1998 and became its president in 2012. He also spent a few years in the UK, and received a PhD from Imperial College London.
Since Xi's anti-corruption drive in 2012, more than two million individuals have been disciplined for cases related to "pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance", according to the party.
Specific charges are often not made public, and broad allegations about disciplinary and legal violations have become routine in the crackdown.
Analysts note that corruption also extends to ideological impurity - or simply put, disloyalty.
Party discipline took centre stage at the fifth plenum last month, which had the most empty seats ever seen after a record 33 members were expelled from the party's central committee.
Chen's ongoing probe suggests that the crackdown is not slowing down.
Shanghai's communist party standing committee said in a statement that its members "unanimously expressed their firm support" for the decision of the party.
The investigation of Chen, the committee said, shows that "the fight against corruption will not stop".

articles.title_orig: China launches Shenzhou-24 crew, setting up a year-long orbital stay for one astronaut
articles.title_zh: China launches Shenzhou-24 crew, setting up a year-long orbital stay for one astronaut
articles.content_orig:
China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts — two Chinese and a Pakistani — sending the first foreign crew member to its space station .
Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, is flying alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, after the craft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday morning. It successfully separated from a rocket and entered its predetermined orbit.
The launch marked the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.
Hours earlier, crowds of people attended a send-off ceremony, with many holding up their phones to capture the moment.
The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during their mission, official Chinese news agency Xinhua earlier reported. Ali will conduct a photosynthetic cyanobacteria experiment in orbit during his short-term mission before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, it said.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of their mission.
"Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space," he said on X on Tuesday.
The joint flight is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.
While this was the first spaceflight for Ali and Wu, Tang has flown on two previous missions and is set to become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, national broadcaster CCTV said.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said that differences in language, culture and psychology had made learning to work together more challenging on this mission, but that both sides' efforts were paying off.
In front of reporters, those efforts were reflected in Ali's Mandarin proficiency. He cited a line of Chinese poetry about climbing one story higher to see farther.
"It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights," he said in Mandarin.
Speaking in English, he said he hoped the next chapter of space cooperation between the two countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the moon, Mars and beyond.
In May, China launched Shenzhou 23 , which carried three astronauts, including one crew member who was set to remain in space for about a year.
China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030. The U.S. is widely seen as China's main space rival, with NASA aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

articles.title_orig: ‘Everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy’: Why Ukraine’s Med strike is a problem for Meloni
articles.title_zh: ‘Everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy’: Why Ukraine’s Med strike is a problem for Meloni
articles.content_orig:
Giorgia Meloni has a Ukraine problem.
With a national Italian election possible as early as this spring, Kyiv’s weekend strikes on a Russian warship and cargo vessel in Libya risk sparking a backlash in Rome — a Kyiv ally that also has traditionally close ties with the North African country.
“If this is a continuation of the war between Russia and Ukraine just a few hundred kilometers from Italy, this is worrying, especially because we work for the stability of Libya,” said Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, who added that Rome had not been informed ahead of time about the attack.
The Italian foreign ministry said Tajani spoke with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday.
"The Minister reiterated to his Ukrainian counterpart how vital it is for Italy to continue working to prevent the conflict with Russia from spreading to the Mediterranean as well," the ministry said in a statement . For Italy, "it is essential to respect Libya’s sovereignty and to continue working towards the country’s stability, unity and sovereignty."
Matteo Salvini, the leader of the far-right League, a pro-Kremlin junior partner in Meloni’s governing coalition, that opposes further military aid to Ukraine said that “it wouldn't make sense” if military support provided to Ukraine “ends up making wars and sinking ships around the world.”
Kyiv defended its right to strike Russian vessels — even those docked in Benghazi, thousands of kilometers away from the battlefield.
The issue threatens to become a headache for Meloni.
Rome is especially concerned about destabilizing Libya, a former Italian colony, fearing that if the politically fragile country collapses into disorder again, it could spark a migration wave across the Mediterranean.
Russia and its allies in Libya could use migration as a weapon against the country, said Arturo Varvelli, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations.
“For Italy, Libya is the most important foreign policy dossier because everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy,” said Lia Quartapelle, a center-left Democratic Party lawmaker and vice chair of the Foreign and European Affairs Committee of Italy’s parliament.
Meloni's strong backing for Ukraine puts her at odds with part of her coalition, as well as with large parts of the political opposition.
This summer, former Italian Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte, leader of the populist 5Star Movement, a key opposition party, set off a political firestorm by questioning further military aid to Ukraine if the center-left wins the next election.
The far-right opposition National Future Party, led by former Gen. Roberto Vannacci, also opposes military aid to Ukraine.
The public is also skeptical. Italians are the least likely to support Ukraine among major Western European countries, with a YouGov survey earlier this year finding that only 32% of Italians care if it wins against Russia.
For Meloni, "it’s a difficult match to handle," said pollster Lorenzo Pregliasco. "We [Italians] are afraid to take sides; we tend to be wary of conflict and of any Italian involvement in any conflict whatsoever."
That national caution has made Italy a relatively small donor to Ukraine — giving far less than countries like Germany or Nordic nations. Italy has provided around €3 billion in military aid, boosted by a new €800 million package.
Although there is worry about blowback, military giving "is unlikely to be affected in a meaningful way by the Ukrainian attacks," said Alessandro Marrone, who leads the defense, security and space program at Rome’s Istituto Affari Internazionali.
And it's not just Italy that is worried about a widening war in the Mediterranean.
“Greece’s government is concerned that the war in Ukraine could open another front in the eastern Mediterranean and is planning to have discussions on the issue with like-minded partners in the near future,” a senior Greek government official said.
Despite the turmoil in Rome and Athens, Kyiv stands by its decision to attack Russian ships.
“Ukraine is defending itself against the armed aggression of the Russian Federation. Our actions constitute the exercise of the inherent right to self-defense," Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters on Tuesday.
"Ukraine has the full right to strike the aggressor’s legitimate military targets. These include Russian warships, cargo vessels transporting military equipment and resources, and tankers belonging to the shadow fleet that sustain Russia’s war machine," he said. "Ukraine is not dragging anyone into the war, nor is it exporting the conflict elsewhere."
There is another risk for Meloni: that Ukraine ends up showing the lack of an Italian strategy in Libya to deal with the Russian presence there, said Varvelli, the ECFR researcher. The Russian naval vessel was sunk in the eastern Libyan port of Benghazi, controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army is allied with Moscow.
"The Ukrainians are simply bringing to light the significant Russian presence in Libya, which consists of six bases and between 1,000 and 1,500 personnel," he said, warning that Italy is “purely reactive” to what is happening in the country.
Veronika Melkozerova reported from Kyiv and Nektaria Stamouli contributed reporting from Athens.

articles.title_orig: Trump Weighs Fresh Tariffs on India and China: What is Behind the US Trade Investigation?
articles.title_zh: Trump Weighs Fresh Tariffs on India and China: What is Behind the US Trade Investigation?
articles.content_orig:
For a minute there, it seemed like someone in the Trump administration might actually be willing to stand up to China.
For about a week and a half, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was the face of an emerging harder line on Nvidia over the potential risks its co-founder Jensen Huang 's affairs posed to national security. Bessent was giving voice to China hawks who had felt sidelined by the Trump administration's willingness to sell artificial intelligence chips to  China.
They see China's AI program as a major threat, and want to restrain its growth by cutting off the supply of advanced chips to China. The resignation of Huang, who pressed the Trump Administration to allow the exports, seemed to signal that the hawks had found new influence in Washington.
By this weekend, Bessent had softened his public resistance to Huang's reinstatement. That came just in time for Nvidia's board to reappoint Huang as CEO at President Donald Trump 's urging.
Whether any real damage was done to national security isn't clear. But it is safe to say that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress won't take Trump at his word when he said on CNBC Monday that the Department of Justice "did a pretty good investigation" that exonerated Huang.
Congress will look deeply into the worries Bessent himself raised about Huang's acknowledged romantic relationship with a woman The New York Times and others have reported was a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia's board said it had received assurances from top U.S. officials and had concluded his return wasn't a national security risk.
A top concern is whether China was able to use the affair to help divert Nvidia's high-end artificial intelligence chips toward helping its military. Bessent in a Nov. 13 interview with CNBC outlined the stakes.
"Any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts the — it hurts our great companies and in the AI race it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Bessent said that his department and others had wanted to blacklist Megaspeed, the company previously run by Alice Huang, Jensen Huang's paramour. But "Commerce has the pen," Bessent said.
The Commerce Department is headed by Secretary Howard Lutnick, Bessent's rival.
Putting Huang back at Nvidia wasn't originally Bessent's preference. He said in a Fox interview on Nov. 15 that the board should "go outside the company" to find a new leader. But by this past weekend, Bessent had apparently gotten on board with Trump's wishes.
"Jensen is on the outside now," Bessent told CBS on Sunday, in trying to explain his apparent policy shift.
Commerce has since taken steps to tighten some restrictions meant to prevent U.S. chips from helping China advance in the AI race.
But there is bipartisan worry about the Nvidia episode. "I think we need to catalog the damage that's been done," Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., told The Wall Street Journal . He said Lutnick had not responded to letters he sent saying the administration should be "taking the threats of communist China more seriously."
But Trump has clearly put an upper limit on how aggressively anyone in his administration can push back on China. The president said Monday that he was swayed by the pageantry in his visit to China last week.
Xi "met me at the plane, which is something they've never done, which was a sign," Trump said.
Trump said he felt like he needed to intervene to back Huang because the stock market was plummeting in the wake of Nvidia's troubles — a development he also blamed on Democrats' midterm victory.
"I watched our country lose $5 trillion because of a bad election," he said. "If I didn't get involved, you'd probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come." Now, its stock performance will be "unbelievable."
Bessent on Sunday played down the market risks. The company "continues to be fantastically profitable, and there is near unlimited demand for their chips worldwide," he told CBS.
Lutnick has embraced Trump's transactional urges. He has backed deals in which the U.S. takes equity stakes in companies such as Intel, saying the taxpayer deserves some of the upside.
Lutnick in January said he had heard Huang pitch Trump on allowing Nvidia to sell its relatively more advanced H200 chips into China.
"There are strong — two sides. We shouldn't sell them any or we should sell them." Where does he stand? "Right in the middle," Lutnick told Bloomberg . Trump decided to go ahead with the deal.
Bessent has said he is "neither a hawk nor a dove" on China, and is simply trying to manage the ultra-sensitive relationship between the world's two biggest economies. But the upshot of the Huang affair seems to be that Bessent wasn't able to sway the president on a matter that seemed cut-and-dried just days ago.
Lutnick, meanwhile, is riding high.
Trump said he discussed whether Huang should return to Nvidia with Lutnick, Bessent and Vice President JD Vance. "Howard Lutnick was very good. Very, he's very professional," Trump said on CNBC Monday.
"I call them the opposites, Scott and Howard," Trump added, before declaring them "both good."

articles.title_orig: Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s new biology skills wow scientists
articles.title_zh: Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s new biology skills wow scientists
articles.content_orig:

            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
Accurately predicting protein structures has been the preserve of specialist AI tools like AlphaFold — but now general-purpose models are catching up. Credit: EMBL-EBI (CC0)
Earlier this month, Xinming Tu set out to test what artificial-intelligence models know about proteins. Tu, a researcher at an AI biology company called Phylo in South San Francisco, California, asked large language models (LLMs) from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google to predict the sequences of obscure bacterial proteins.
He left the analysis to run overnight and woke up shocked at the results. The latest versions of Anthropic’s Claude models had outperformed other LLMs — but also specialized ‘protein language models’, which are trained on vast troves of sequence data and specially designed for such tasks.
Scientists are using AI to dream up revolutionary new proteins
Scientists are using AI to dream up revolutionary new proteins
When Tu and Leo Chen, a computational biologist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts, shared the results in a 16 November blogpost , it set off a frenzy among computational biologists to see what other protein biology LLMs such as Claude could do. For instance, Tu and Chen and others have found it could perform a key step in protein-structure prediction.
And on 24 November, OpenAI announced that its latest language models had successfully designed new proteins, some of which behaved as expected when made and tested in the lab. The results hint that the latest LLMs might be gaining a sophisticated understanding of protein biology.
The research has kicked off a debate over the future of biological AI . Some scientists predict that ‘general purpose’ models such as Claude and ChatGPT will eventually outperform specialist tools such as AlphaFold at tasks including protein structure prediction and design.
“We want to see a world where a scientist can just describe in natural language what they want a ChatGPT model to do, and the model can just be infinitely flexible and design exactly what the person wants,” says Joy Jiao, who leads life-sciences research at OpenAI in San Francisco, California.
But some researchers question the extent to which LLMs are learning underlying lessons in protein biology. They suggest that some of their abilities could be the result of regurgitating training data.
The release of AlphaFold2, Google DeepMind’s blockbuster protein-structure-prediction AI , in 2020 launched a revolution in biological AI. There is now a vast ecosystem of software — much of it open source — for modelling different properties of proteins, such as how they interact with possible drugs, and for designing new proteins.
Researchers have begun using LLMs to orchestrate these specialist models, but it has mostly been as a time-saving measure, says Martin Pačesa, a structural biologist at the University of Zurich. “In most cases, a specialist will always perform better than a generalist for a given task,” he says.
Five protein-design questions that still challenge AI
Five protein-design questions that still challenge AI
To see if an LLM could stand in for specialist protein-design tools, Jiao and her colleagues asked an OpenAI model called GPT-6.2 to design 3D protein structures capable of binding to five different biological targets, including proteins implicated in cancer and immune disorders. After the LLMs generated the designs, the researchers used a specialist AI tool to determine a corresponding genetic sequence. Lab experiments confirmed that around 11% of designs were able to bind their target.
In other experiments, the OpenAI team showed that its LLMs could design protein sequences, redesign existing antibodies, and other tasks typically performed by specialist tools. In some cases, the LLM performed as well as some specialist tools, and in others, such as predicting the 3D structure of proteins, it was far off. OpenAI researchers describe the work in a blogpost and technical paper .
Jiao emphasizes that the work is a proof of principle, and that specialized AI tools were still needed for key steps. But Masatoshi Uehara, an OpenAI researcher who was part of the effort, believes that LLMs will only get better at protein biology. “I believe the large language model can technically beat every specialized model in even each capability,” he says.

articles.title_orig: China's Huawei says US conviction 'without legal or factual merit'
articles.title_zh: China's Huawei says US conviction 'without legal or factual merit'
articles.content_orig:
A United States jury has convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.
However, jurors on Tuesday acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge is typically used in organised crime and drug cases, but prosecutors used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to steal intellectual property from US companies.
The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which US prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the US and elsewhere.
Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to US sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to US government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.
US authorities had targeted Huawei for years, saying the company posed national security risks.
The criminal case began in 2018, and the following year the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology.
Experts have said the case has not undermined Huawei’s business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China’s push for artificial intelligence.
The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defence calling 15.
Huawei and three affiliates faced 12 charges, including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice.
Lawyers for the company said US investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei’s more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that did not actually exist.
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but saw the racketeering conspiracy acquittal as vindication.
“That was the only count that brought all of the allegations together,” and the jury rejected it, he said outside court, saying that the verdict “repudiated the central government narrative in the case”.
It is unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei’s global fortunes. The company hasn’t been allowed to sell equipment to US carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and the United Kingdom.
The case emerged in December 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and daughter of the company’s founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada.
Meng had been secretly indicted for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions.
She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero’s welcome. The charges against her were dropped.
The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran.
Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.
During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel’s antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.
Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.
Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng’s deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.
The defence argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei’s business in Iran and were competing for Huawei’s business.
Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having “cherry-picked” a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy.
He said Huawei succeeded through “hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development”.
Huawei has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

articles.title_orig: U.S.-China tensions could rise in 2027, but China could keep growing its exports: Economist
articles.title_zh: U.S.-China tensions could rise in 2027, but China could keep growing its exports: Economist
articles.content_orig:
China is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.
On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India .
China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.
It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense.
Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.
The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.
The thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.
Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.
Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.
Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.
Another flash point was when Beijing put export controls on tunnel boring machines last month. "Our relations with China remain good, and if there aren't any new hurdles , they can improve further," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal reportedly said after China's move to tighten TBM exports.
On Monday, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson reportedly said Beijing is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both sides amid reports that fewer Indian businessmen got visas to attend an annual trade fair in Shanghai.
The Chinese "actively disrupt" areas where India is trying to make progress in terms of moving global supply chains, developing advanced industrial technologies such as EVs, batteries, electronic components, and pharmaceutical ingredients, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC.
He added China is increasingly focused on containing India economically rather than through military overtures.
India's manufacturing push still relies on Chinese inputs, from electronics components and solar materials to rare earth magnets and specialized machinery. Between April and October, India imported goods worth $96.6 billion from China , up more than 30% from a year ago, as per commerce ministry data released earlier this month.
Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products.
While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.

articles.title_orig: Trump says pardon is always an option for Jensen Huang, and that pleading the Fifth isn’t necessary
articles.title_zh: Trump says pardon is always an option for Jensen Huang, and that pleading the Fifth isn’t necessary
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said that while pardoning Jensen Huang for any potential criminal activity remains an option, he doesn’t think that will be needed for the newly reinstated Nvidia CEO .
“It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” Trump told the New York Post in an interview published Tuesday night.
Asked about Huang’s scheduled appearances next week on Capitol Hill, Trump said, “I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people.”
“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person,” the president said.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on Trump’s comments. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.
Speaking at a news conference Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated he would have told Trump if Huang had been involved in any criminal activity.
“To the extent that, that the department, that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that is, that is, that’s just not, that’s something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true,” Blanche said.
In Congress, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are preparing to grill Huang over their national security concerns.
A spokesperson for the Republican-led House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement “changes nothing” and that there “are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers.”
Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are expected to sit for transcribed interviews next Tuesday and Wednesday before the House Select Committee on China, the House Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Huang, who has not been charged with a crime, resigned from his post as CEO of the chip giant following reports that he had a relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies believed was a Chinese spy. In a Nov. 8 memo to Nvidia’s staff, he said, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Trump worked behind the scenes over the weekend to get Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back. That move has been met with bipartisan backlash.
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., on Monday raised concerns over Nvidia’s quick reversal to rehire Huang after indicating it wouldn’t.
“His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement,” Ricketts wrote in a post on X.
Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., wrote that with Nvidia’s rehiring of Huang, “the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens.”
Cramer and Ricketts are both members of the Senate Banking Committee, where Huang is scheduled to testify in public Dec. 3.
In celebrating Huang’s return, Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social post that the U.S. government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”
Similarly, Nvidia’s board said it reached the decision to reinstate Huang after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Trump open to pardoning Jensen Huang if needed: NY Post
articles.title_zh: Trump open to pardoning Jensen Huang if needed: NY Post
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said he would be willing to pardon reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if needed after Huang appears before Congress next week, according to an exclusive interview with the New York Post.
Huang's reinstatement followed Trump's intervention with Nvidia's board, including a reported call into a board meeting to argue for his return. Even so, lawmakers are still set to scrutinize his relationship with suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang in two appearances next week.
Nvidia shares surged 31% on Monday after Huang was reinstated as CEO, before falling 5.9% on Tuesday amid a broader market pullback.
Trump also said that Huang should not need to invoke the Fifth Amendment to avoid self-incrimination when he appears for a closed-door interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Dec. 1 and before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.
"I think it's an interesting story for people," Trump said, according to the NY Post. "I think I want him to just tell the truth."
Trump added that while a pardon was "always an option," he did not think it would be "necessary," the newspaper reported. The president's clemency authority is limited to federal offenses, according to the Justice Department's Office of the Pardon Attorney.
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told Fox News on Monday that he expected Huang to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights during the congressional proceedings.
"I expect him to take the Fifth Amendment so he doesn't incriminate himself in criminal prosecution, but we're going to give him a chance to explain," Kennedy said.
Trump also told the New York Post that he was open to the U.S. government taking an equity stake in Nvidia, similar to its stake in Intel in 2025, arguing that the company's success was vital to maintaining the U.S. lead in artificial intelligence.
He also said it was his understanding that Huang had not had affairs with other women linked to Beijing and that he did not know how many affairs Huang had acknowledged.
Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., the lead Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, told CNBC on Tuesday that he believed Trump was making decisions that could benefit his own stock portfolio, despite the president's assertion that he does not make trades himself.
"If you don't believe that, you're too innocent to be let out of the house by yourself. The whole thing is a money-making operation. What's the alternative explanation?" Raskin said.
Separately, independent journalist Marisa Kabas reported that Huang told Nvidia employees at Tuesday's all-hands meeting that Trump "loves" the company because of its employees' "contributions" to the U.S., while also addressing questions about whether Nvidia had become political or partisan.
"I want to be very clear: President Trump is the United States president. I'll do everything I can to help this president be informed about how he can make decisions in the best interests of the country," Huang said.
The reinstated CEO added that it would be a "great honor and a privilege" to go to Washington, D.C., to "inform them so the government can make the best possible decision," and said he would do the same for whoever becomes the next president.
"Don't think for a second politics played a role in the company. We are the most apolitical company. Everything he's done is because of his affection, admiration, and recognition of the great company that you are," Huang said.
