articles.title_orig: Yemen’s Houthis Take Second Swipe at Tallest Tower in Saudi Capital
articles.title_zh: Yemen’s Houthis Take Second Swipe at Tallest Tower in Saudi Capital
articles.content_orig:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis hit Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund Public Investment Fund Tower on Tuesday, injuring 11.
The kingdom's civil defense directorate did not name the tower, but posted an image showing damage to the PIF tower. Eyewitness reports by Al Jazeera also indicated that the building that was hit was the PIF Tower in Riyadh.
The injured included two Saudi citizens, two Indians, three Nepalis, and four Egyptians.
The attack comes as tensions have flared up again between Saudi Arabia, which is leading an international coalition to restore the internationally recognized government of Yemen after it was forced to flee in 2015, and the Houthis.
Turki al-Maliki , a spokesperson for the coalition, said one of the towers of the financial center was targeted in a "cowardly terrorist attack," referring to the financial center in the Saudi capital of Riyadh.
He added that authorities were conducting an on-site investigation at the scene of the attack.
This has been the second attack by the Iran-backed group in six days on the tower, although the previous attack did not cause any casualties.
On Wednesday, Houthi brigadier general Yahya Saree warned on X that the port of Jeddah and all Saudi ports along the Red Sea coast will become "targets for our forces," if Riyadh attacks the Yemeni Red Sea port of Hodeidah.
The coalition had asked civilians to evacuate the port "for their safety," on Nov. 20.
Attacks by the rebel Houthis have been escalating on Saudi Arabia, with the group targeting one of Saudi Arabia's oil refineries on Sunday , according to Reuters. The Houthis also launched drone and ballistic missiles against the country's airports, most recently targeting the King Khalid International Airport on Oct. 25 , according to reports.
The new attacks come amid wider strikes by Tehran and Iran-linked forces in the Gulf, with Bahrain also reporting that it was attacked by Iran over the weekend. Bahrain is home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet.
"As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site," Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said on X.
The ministry later said two people , a Bahraini citizen and a Pakistani resident, were injured in the attack.
— CNBC's Azhar Sukri contributed to this report.

articles.content_orig:
SALT LAKE CITY — Utah Sen. John Curtis said he agreed with tech CEO Jensen Huang's initial decision to step down from Nvidia and appeared skeptical about Huang's sudden reinstatement this week.
Huang's surprise comeback as head of one of the world's most prominent chip manufacturers was met with bipartisan pushback. Huang initially left the company after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump took credit for Huang's return to Nvidia. But the move prompted skepticism from some in Washington, including Curtis.
"Nvidia's board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk," the Republican senator wrote on X. "I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?"
He added that Huang's initial decision to leave Nvidia after news of the affair broke was the right call.
"Just 11 days after Nvidia announced his departure, the board brought him back while its own independent investigation was still underway," Curtis continued. "Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him. I'd like to know what changed."
Meanwhile, Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, has been quiet on social media about Huang and the controversy surrounding his role at Nvidia. A spokesperson did not immediately respond Tuesday when asked if Lee had any comment on Huang's reinstatement at the tech company.
Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, a Republican who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, called for Congress to investigate the situation.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," he wrote on social media. "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company that is a customer of Nvidia. The alleged spy Huang had an affair with is a former executive for the company.
During a company-wide meeting Tuesday, Huang apologized to employees for making "some terrible mistakes," according to the New York Times , but he challenged the notion that he was back only because Trump pushed for it.
The president's involvement in the issue has raised questions about Nvidia's independence at a time when many are worried about a race with China to develop artificial general intelligence.
"In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company," Peter Cohan, associate professor of management practice at Babson College in Massachusetts, told the Associated Press . "That's because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it."
Former Utah Sen. Mitt Romney also weighed in on the latest AI developments on Tuesday, referring to the reported sales of AI chips to China.
"Let me get this straight: we rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they'd need to get ahead of us," Romney wrote on X. "Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse."
The U.S. Department of Commerce has approved selling more than 800,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies this year, including companies with ties to the Chinese military, the New York Times reported last week. On Sunday, before Huang was renamed CEO, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for answers about Nvidia's chip sales to China.
"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers," he told CBS' "Face the Nation."

articles.title_orig: Team Trump Plans New Wave Of US Tariffs, India, China On Hit List: Report
articles.title_zh: Team Trump Plans New Wave Of US Tariffs, India, China On Hit List: Report
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
GUANGZHOU, China — Behind the scenes, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spent months pushing for action that would signal resolve within the Trump administration against China’s pursuit of the most powerful American computer chips, a flashpoint  in their race for superiority in artificial intelligence, multiple sources said.
But President Trump’s courtship of Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, seeking to alleviate tensions between the world’s greatest powers, and a contingent of advisors skeptical of commercial warfare against Beijing slowed the process down — giving China months of opportunity to gain access to U.S. semiconductors through the back door.
Ultimately, just hours before departing for Asia alongside  Trump, Bessent got his way, bolstering his position ahead of talks with Chinese officials in Shenzhen this week on the risks posed by frontier systems.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit: that Washington is serious about curbing Chinese circumvention — and that China hawks within the administration may be gaining the upper hand.
Trump has repeatedly sidestepped confrontation with Xi over the intensifying AI race in their two previous meetings this year, in Beijing and Washington, wary of upsetting a carefully managed detente and reluctant to jeopardize a technology boom increasingly central to the U.S. economy.
The new rules restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best AI models.
But the administration, from the president down, is acutely aware of China’s ambitions to dominate an industry that could reshape the global balance of power. That competitive drive was underscored this month by a scandal involving a Chinese espionage campaign targeting Jensen Huang, co-founder of Nvidia, the world’s leading AI chip maker.
Before resigning from the company in disgrace Thursday, Huang admitted to having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy — a woman who worked at a firm in Singapore accused by American authorities of helping to divert restricted Nvidia chips to China, in violation of U.S. export controls.
The national security scandal has roiled the markets — and in so doing, commanded Trump’s attention — inflicting a significant devaluation on Nvidia and reverberating well beyond it, wiping nearly $1 trillion from the combined market value of major technology companies in a single trading session on Monday.
Trump, who counts Huang a friend and ally, indicated he would be open to his return as Nvidia’s chief executive. Bessent suggested otherwise, expressing confidence its board could find competent new leadership and urging a full investigation.
Huang indicated his interest Tuesday in returning to Nvidia, writing in a social media post that “I would be honored” to resume his role as CEO if asked by the board of directors. But Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said later Tuesday that the company does not intend to bring Huang back.
Trump is not expected to raise the Nvidia matter directly with Xi. But Bessent plans to do so in his own meetings, one official said.
The Treasury secretary has thus taken on the role of an enforcer, pursuing a tougher line than Trump is willing to take himself in his highly personalized relationship with the Chinese leader.
Bessent is scheduled to meet with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on the sidelines of the summitry in Shenzhen to discuss potential collaboration on AI safety protocols, standards for testing of advanced models, and a direct communications channel for AI emergencies.
The two men have met before to discuss AI, most recently in New York, where they agreed in principle to coordinate. But the talks have yet to produce much in the way of tangible results.
“Bessent is signaling that, while he sees working with Beijing to mitigate AI risks as a priority, it won’t come at the expense of actions that he sees as necessary to protect U.S. national security, like limiting AI chip exports to China,” said Daniel Remler, a senior fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
The administration’s latest action marks a policy defeat for Howard Lutnick , secretary of the Commerce Department, who oversees chip policy and had advocated for a less restrictive approach than Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative.
The feud began spilling into public view ahead of the president’s travel, and in light of the Nvidia scandal, after Bessent said in a television interview that the Commerce Department “has the pen” to act, implying a split within the team.
“Look, there’re two different views,” Trump told reporters Monday, answering questions on the matter. “One view is you don’t want to insult China. We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.”
“The other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do,” Trump continued. “You can’t say either is wrong or right. We’ll let you know.”
Beyond the diplomatic niceties, Trump has been explicit and consistent since resuming office that the United States must “win” the race for AI superiority, calling the alternative “not acceptable.”
“Whoever wins AI,” Trump said at the United Nations General Assembly in September, “whoever wins superintelligence, wins.”
Trump will arrive in China on Wednesday after meeting with world leaders in Manila, including those from the Quad — an alliance of Japan, India, Australia and the United States —  who discussed AI at their own summit Tuesday evening.
Describing “superintelligence” — Trump’s preferred term for AI — as “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution,” Trump announced a Quad effort to accelerate adoption of the technology, including an investment of more than $85 million to enhance AI ecosystems throughout the region.
“We want to be careful with it,” Trump said, “but it’s amazing, the things that have come out, in terms of science and in terms of medical breakthroughs. No one can believe what we’re finding. And we’re finding it fast.”
“We want to be very careful, but we want to cherish it,” he added. “The United States as you know is leading in that capacity, by quite a bit.”
As he meets with the leaders of India, Japan and Australia, Trump will face pressure to sustain resolve against Beijing despite his yearlong courtship of President Xi Jinping.
The new U.S. rule requires overseas data centers serving customers in China, Russia, Iran and Cuba to identify their end users before gaining access to chips. It also imposes additional licensing requirements on chip sales to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the Commerce Department identifies as posing a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to unauthorized destinations.
U.S. officials say that export controls are not up for negotiation in talks with the Chinese. But Beijing sees them as yet another historic example of Washington trying to contain its rise — a posture that has repeatedly stifled diplomatic progress between the two superpowers.
“While administration officials say export controls aren’t up for negotiation, Chinese officials will certainly bring them up,” Remler said. “These restrictions are the key obstacle to China’s AI progress, which is increasingly important to the Chinese economy and to Xi’s strategic goals.”
China claims it does not seek an all-powerful, generalized “superintelligence,” but rather specialized AI systems embedded across industries to boost productivity and improve quality of life.
In Beijing’s telling, it is the United States — pursuing generalized AI through a private sector largely unchecked by the federal gove

articles.title_orig: I Designed My Dream Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale. It's Ridiculous
articles.title_zh: I Designed My Dream Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale. It's Ridiculous
articles.content_orig:
Ferrari’s new 296 Challenge Stradale is a badass, 670-horsepower, non-hybrid race car for the road. Want one? It’ll cost you around $307,000 before options.
But if you want to get a little fancier with your new Ferrari, the automaker’s online configurator has plenty of ways to customize the supercar. And some of them are pretty wild. I wasted 30 minutes of my day dialing in my perfect 296 CS.
Let’s start with the most important part: paint. Ferrari offers a whopping 35 colors, split into four categories: Standard, Historical, Classic, and Special. You could go with the classic Rosso Corsa or Giallo Modena, but I'm going with something a little different here: Giallo Ambra, aka fancy orange.
Once you pick your paint, Ferrari lets you choose from a handful of livery options, including upper- and lower-body graphics, wing decals, door numbers, and more. Normally, I'd say a livery is mandatory on a car like this. But the 296 Challenge Stradale looks so damn good in a single color that it really doesn't need one.
Ferrari also lets you turn just about anything into carbon fiber. Front splitter? Carbon fiber. Rear diffuser? Carbon fiber. Even the engine covers? That's right, carbon fiber.
If you really want to go crazy, you can replace all the glass with Lexan, a lightweight polycarbonate that's a little lighter than traditional glass. That should help shave off a few pounds. Ferrari will even let you ditch the Prancing Horse badges on the front fenders entirely or swap the metal logos for painted ones.
Ferrari offers six wheel designs for the 296 CS, ranging from light silver to darker gray and black. You can also customize the wheel bolts, center caps, and more. I'm going with Forged Diamond-Polished wheels and titanium wheel bolts.
Depending on how you plan to use your 296 (primarily on road or track), Ferrari offers both Bridgestone and Pirelli tires. There are even two Pirelli "Color Edition" options with yellow or gray accents. We'll pass on those.
Brake calipers are available in eight different colors, ranging from black and red to yellow and silver.
Most of the interior upgrades are pretty subtle. You can choose floor mats with or without logos, pick from 26 stitching colors (we went with Filo Spec Flash Orange to match the exterior), and customize the lower portion of the dashboard with 22 different colors.
Perhaps the most important choice, though, is the seats. Ferrari offers two options: Racing and "Best Weight," as the automaker calls it. The racing seats appear to be lighter and probably less comfortable, but Ferrari doesn't really divulge any specifics.
There are seven different Alcantara colors available, depending on which seats you choose. You can also customize the seatbelts with six different colors, add a central racing stripe, and choose from additional stitching options.
Like most Ferraris, the 296 CS doesn't have a dedicated center touchscreen. That said, Ferrari does offer an optional passenger display, which seems a little odd in a car like this. Maybe your nephew can watch Shrek while you lap COTA. The world is your oyster.
As you'd expect, Ferrari doesn't list prices for any of these options in its configurator. You'll have to contact your local dealer to find out how much any of them will set you back.
But getting into a new 296 Challenge Stradale will cost you at least $307,000 to start. And that's before you start checking boxes.

articles.title_orig: Trump says ‘it’s probably not too late’ for the US to take a stake in Nvidia
articles.title_zh: Trump says ‘it’s probably not too late’ for the US to take a stake in Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump may want a piece of the Nvidia pie.
After saying he intervened to support the reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang , Trump said he has also considered seeking out an equity stake in the chipmaker for the US government.
"I thought about it," Trump told the New York Post on Tuesday. "I said, 'You know, maybe I should do it,' but I didn't bring it up at this point. It's probably not too late."
Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, less than two weeks after resigning from the company he founded when reports emerged of extramarital affairs with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy and an executive who reported to him.
Huang's return came days after Nvidia's board said they had no plans to bring him back. Trump, who has repeatedly praised Huang, played up his role in the CEO's return and said he spoke directly to the board.
The president's suggestion of the government taking an equity stake in Nvidia would align with similar moves made under the current administration. In August 2025, the US government reached a deal to invest $8.9 billion in Intel in exchange for a nearly 10% stake, a move aimed at supporting the semiconductor industry.
Prior to Intel, the administration said it took a "golden share" in US Steel in exchange for approving its acquisition by Nippon Steel, a Japanese company. The government has also invested in critical minerals firms MP Materials, Lithium Americas, and Trilogy Metals, as well as established a strategic partnership with the nuclear energy company Westinghouse.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: US ready to slap tariffs on China, EU and others over subsidized production, AP sources say
articles.title_zh: US ready to slap tariffs on China, EU and others over subsidized production, AP sources say
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and 14 other economies, according to two people familiar with the matter.
The U.S. Trade Representative's Office is expected to release the results of a monthslong tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies by the 16 economies in the coming days, according to the people who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
They stressed the timing for the rollout of the tariffs could still change. The White House and USTR did not respond to requests for comment.
Plans for the new tariffs are part of an effort to replace broader duties the administration set last year that were subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.
The tariffs are in response to what the White House has said is excessive manufacturing output in those countries, boosted by subsidies, that has led to a flood of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies.
The anticipated action constitutes a second step in the administration’s efforts to replace the duties announced in April 2025 that the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional in February. The White House slapped 60 trading partners with levies of 10% to 12.5% in July, charging that they have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.
The anticipated trade action demonstrates that the Trump administration is still willing to impose import taxes despite a sweeping loss for the Republican Party in this month’s midterm elections, fueled largely by affordability concerns as inflation remains elevated. At the same time, the new duties could test how the Democrats will respond to tariffs imposed unilaterally by Trump.
Even with majorities in both the House and Senate, Trump could veto any legislation that overturns or waters down the tariffs.

articles.title_orig: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.
Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.
The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.
The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.
During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.
Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.
For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army  were accounted for in the Rosstat files.
The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.
We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.
Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.
As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.
Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.
Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.
BBC Russian's own detailed records of Russian losses has reached 290,012, verified together with Mediazona from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves. The actual death toll is likely to be higher, as not all deaths are reported publicly.
Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.
According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).
Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.
In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.
At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.
This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.
The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.
The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. Military experts estimate that the BBC's figure of 290,012, gleaned from open sources, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll – ranging from 527,295 to 644,471.
In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.
Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia board joins Jensen Huang under scrutiny after reinstating embattled CEO
articles.title_zh: Nvidia board joins Jensen Huang under scrutiny after reinstating embattled CEO
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump’s Truth Social account is many things: a disturbing stream of consciousness, a nationwide embarrassment, a place where professionalism and discretion (and truth) generally go to die. But, often, the feed is a gallery of self-portraits, many of which have been A.I.-generated. Trump as a pontiff; Trump as a king; Trump as a king and a fighter pilot, dumping sewage on protesters, in a video set to “Danger Zone,” by Kenny Loggins. In this context, the image that Trump posted on Monday —of a blood-splattered Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s newly reinstated C.E.O., victoriously hoisting a brassiere—might barely even register. And yet the photo is an anomaly, not because it’s so vulgar (this is the same account, after all, that once shared a clip of the Obamas as apes) but because it is glorifying someone who is not Donald Trump. If anything, the photo—a play on that photo , the iconic picture taken of Trump after he was nearly assassinated at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania—is a strange self-own, a diminishment of the event that helped Trump reclaim the Presidency, and a reminder of whose interests it is that the White House now serves.
The Lede Reporting and commentary on what you need to know today.
In the picture, which appears to be made with A.I., and posted, without a caption, Trump has been replaced by Huang, and the American flag by a black-and-green Nvidia flag. Huang is raising his fist, just as Trump did, but his fingers are clasped around a red underwire bra—red because bras are seemingly always red in the male imagination but also presumably because Huang’s initial downfall was prompted by allegations that he was sleeping with a suspected Chinese spy. As in the original shot, the man at the center of the picture is still flanked by Secret Service agents, a detail that feels like a lazy holdover; a cleverer meme might have swapped out the agents for Elon Musk and David Sacks, two of Huang’s most high-profile supporters. But perhaps the image of federal protection is apt. Not long after Nvidia announced Huang’s return—an about-face that came just eleven days after his resignation—Trump took credit for the company’s decision to bring Huang back. “I convinced them,” he told CNBC, in a hallucinatory, nearly hour-long phone interview. “I made the deal.” He noted, “We have to protect our geniuses, and he’s certainly a genius.”
It is ironic, to say the least, that one of the most anti-science Presidents in recent memory—one who has gutted university funding ; waged war against individual scientists, such as Anthony Fauci; and tried to make it much harder , through visa fees and restrictions, for immigrant scientists to study and work in America—is now claiming that he wants to protect geniuses. But it is true that Trump has consistently worked to protect Jensen Huang. On November 8th, Nvidia, the world’s biggest chip company, announced that it was opening an investigation into Huang, who had been romantically involved with a woman determined by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. (China has denied that the woman, Alice Huang, is a spy, but the Times recently reported that she “kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year,” during her relationship with the Nvidia C.E.O.) Trump was quick to describe Huang as “an honorable guy” who “probably has an excuse for it.” After talking to Huang, Trump explained, “He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him.” (Never mind that, this past May, the Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, reportedly warned Trump about Alice Huang.)
Trump urged Huang not to step down from his role at Nvidia, but when Huang stepped down anyway, on November 12th—following reports of two more alleged extramarital affairs with non-spies, both of whom worked under him at Nvidia—Trump briefly pivoted to championing another genius. He suggested that the former Apple C.E.O. Tim Cook, a man whom Trump once referred to as “Tim Apple,” take Huang’s place. (“A Legend replaces a Legend!” Trump wrote, on Truth Social.) Unfortunately, the markets weren’t as optimistic about Nvidia’s future; the company’s stock price dropped more than sixteen per cent. Suddenly, Trump was on Fox News, saying that “we have to take care of our geniuses,” because “we don’t have that many of them.” On Monday, CNBC asked Trump whether the stock-market losses had prompted his intervention on behalf of Huang. Trump replied, “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term. The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me.”
In any case, after Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang, citing “input from senior levels of the United States government” in its announcement, the company’s shares surged more than thirty per cent. “The response from the market has been very positive,” Trump told the Wall Street Journal on Monday evening. “That really shows the decision was right.”
Trump’s obsession with the stock market isn’t new, although it has likely been amplified by recent events. The President, reeling from his party’s sweeping defeat in the midterm elections —a nationwide repudiation of his Administration’s policies and priorities, which have exacerbated the affordability crisis across the country—appears determined to avoid a stock-market collapse and an A.I.-bubble burst, outcomes that would further tank his standing in the final years of his Presidency. Perhaps even more significant are Trump’s personal financial ties with Nvidia. A Washington Post investigation found that the President’s holdings in the company ballooned to as much as sixty-two million dollars’ worth of stock before Huang’s scandals became public, with the value of those holdings appreciating amid a series of policy decisions and relaxing of restrictions that benefitted Nvidia’s bottom line. Huang has seemingly become one of Trump’s closest corporate allies not through a mutual quest to enhance American infrastructure, or to improve the country’s economic condition, but through their overlapping personal and financial interests. Genius recognizes genius.
Still, one assumes—or hopes—that Trump would be at least marginally alarmed by Huang’s entanglements with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. This is a President who, during his first term, instigated a trade war with China, persistently portraying Xi Jinping’s government as ruthlessly hostile to the U.S., and used a similar justification for implementing further tariffs on the country during his second term. Alice Huang isn’t just thought to have been a spy for the Chinese government; during her relationship with Jensen Huang, she also worked for the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, one of the largest purchasers of Nvidia chips, which is alleged to have helped Chinese customers circumvent U.S. export controls. Last year, Trump told “60 Minutes” that no country “other than the United States” would have access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips. Megaspeed is the subject of a U.S. Justice Department probe into whether it facilitated the flow of advanced chips to China. (Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.)
In recent months, however, we’ve seen Trump’s antagonistic posture toward China soften. He’s been bragging about his “outstanding” relationship with Xi, and dismissing concerns about Chinese espionage and possible national-security threats. “Somebody said, ‘Oh, they spy on us,’ ” Trump recalled during a September exchange with reporters in the Oval Office. “And I said, ‘Maybe they do, but we spy on them, too.’ ” Trump took a similar tack in his CNBC interview on Monday, arguing that it didn’t matter if Alice Huang was in touch with China’s Ministry of State Security, since Trump himself was in contact with the agency, too. Pointing to his recent summit with Xi in Shenzhen, Trump said, laughing, “I’m involved also if you really get down to it, right?” As if a diplomatic meeting between two heads of state were at all comparab

articles.title_orig: Incoming Democratic chairs demand answers from Trump on Huang’s reinstatement
articles.title_zh: Incoming Democratic chairs demand answers from Trump on Huang’s reinstatement
articles.content_orig:
Republican pushback to Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO is growing, despite President Donald Trump earlier downplaying any blowback from his party.
The chairs of the GOP-led House intelligence and foreign affairs committees as well as the House select committee on the Chinese Communist Party criticized Nvidia in a joint statement on Monday. Reps. Rick Crawford, Brian Mast and John Moolenaar said the company’s “brief internal investigation” and reinstatement of Huang “do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed.”
GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan of North Carolina also blasted Huang’s reinstatement as a “mistake.”
Is Nvidia’s CEO too big to fail?
“Today, we sent a signal that one man’s financial impact on our economy outweighs the importance of good governance, good citizenship, and adherence to the law,” the North Carolina Republican wrote in a post on X . “That is a dangerous precedent to set, and one I believe will come at a significant cost to our country in the long run.”
GOP Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota wrote , “The legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens.”
Sen. John Curtis of Utah went as far as to scrutinize the input Nvidia said it received from “senior levels of the United States government” that Huang poses no national security risk.
“Nvidia’s board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk. I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” Curtis said .
Arkansas GOP Sen. Tom Cotton, who is known as a China hawk, said in a post on X that Congress must investigate further and called for his chip export bill to pass.
“The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” said Cotton, who is the outgoing Senate Intelligence Committee chairman. “Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other.”
That legislation proposes requiring some kind of “location verification mechanism” on advanced chips and directs the Commerce Department to study “other potential chip security mechanisms.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Monday evening, however, refused to answer during an interview with Fox News whether Huang had been cleared of any national security concerns or potential legal violations before being reinstated.
CNN reported earlier Monday that several other Republicans have criticized or questioned the move to reinstate Huang — including Sens. John Cornyn and Pete Ricketts and Rep. Don Bacon.
Earlier Monday in an interview with CNBC, Trump dismissed any concerns from GOP lawmakers saying, “When I speak to them, they’re going to be great.”
This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: Jim Cramer sizes up six retail stocks after earnings — and names his two favorites
articles.title_zh: Jim Cramer sizes up six retail stocks after earnings — and names his two favorites
articles.content_orig:
CNBC's Jim Cramer on Tuesday assessed the latest earnings reports from six major retailers, identifying which stocks have more room to run.
Retail stocks have been a bright spot the last few months as investors rotated out of technology stocks and oil prices and interest rates retreated from their highs. The SPDR S&P Retail ETF (XRT) has gained 9% this quarter, while the Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) has plunged nearly 20% and the S&P 500 has shed almost 6%.
"Retailer earnings went great today, with all six major retailers that I was watching gaining ground, and several — including Dollar Tree, Dick's, Kohl's and Abercrombie & Fitch — notching strong double-digit gains," the " Mad Money " host said.
"That said, some reports were better than others," he added. "Burlington Stores and Kohl's basically just beat low expectations, Dick's had a nice bounce-back quarter, and Dollar Tree was very solid. But Best Buy and Abercrombie & Fitch, two of our favorite names in the group, had the best reports of all."
Here's where Cramer stands on each retailer.
Dollar Tree shares surged 11% after the discount retailer beat expectations for comparable sales, revenue and adjusted earnings per share and raised its full-year outlook. "This is a company that's been focused on self-help initiatives recently, and the combination of their progress on that front and the value proposition they can offer ... are driving the strong performance that we've seen from Dollar Tree recently," he said.
Burlington Stores missed comparable sales and revenue expectations while merely matching earnings estimates. Cramer attributed Tuesday's 4% rally to low expectations following a more than 30% decline from its all-time closing high on July 30, as well as the company's largely unchanged fourth-quarter outlook. He still prefers TJX Companies , which delivered a much stronger report last week , and is a holding in Cramer's Charitable Trust .
Dick's Sporting Goods shares jumped almost 15% after the retailer beat on top and bottom lines and raised its full-year earnings outlook. Despite inventory challenges across the athletic footwear and apparel industry, Cramer said Dick's is "controlling what it can control, taking market share while the market is muted, and setting itself up for long-term success."
Best Buy delivered "arguably the best set of numbers from any retailer that reported" despite posting the smallest stock gain of just 3%, Cramer said. Comparable sales rose more than 6%, and the electronics retailer also raised its full-year outlook, projecting comparable sales growth of 2% to 4% for the holiday quarter.
Cramer attributed the muted stock reaction to Best Buy's nearly 80% rally from its 52-week closing low on May 13. "At less than 15 times earnings, with a 3.9% yield and this latest quarter nearly for free, I think Best Buy is still a buy," he said.
Kohl's shares climbed 19% after the department store chain beat comparable sales and earnings expectations, though tariff refunds contributed significantly to the bottom-line beat. Like Burlington, Kohl's benefited from low expectations.
"Kohl's is a funky story," he said. "Credit to them for not doing as badly as the analysts expected them to. But it's still not a business that I'm a long-term believer in."
Abercrombie & Fitch shares surged almost 20% after the apparel retailer topped expectations and raised its full-year outlook. Cramer praised the company's disciplined inventory management, which has supported pricing power and margins.
"ANF can be a boom or bust stock, but right now it's booming, and I don't think it's done going higher," Cramer said.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's Jensen Huang still has security clearance, sources say
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's Jensen Huang still has security clearance, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang still holds a security clearance, multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
Huang has drawn weeks of scrutiny , following reports that he had an affair with a businesswoman and alleged Chinese intelligence asset whose company is suspected of transferring advanced Nvidia chips to China. Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive two weeks ago, but the company's board reinstated him on Monday following direct appeals from President Trump, who said he offered the board an "assurance" that Huang did not pose a national security threat.
Revoking Huang's clearance was discussed, sources said.
Huang never received a defensive security briefing from the administration after he was alerted about businesswoman Alice Huang's alleged ties to China, a source directly familiar with the matter said. Such briefings, also called counterintelligence briefings, help people with a U.S. government security clearance recognize threats.
It is not uncommon for executives at tech companies that do classified federal work to have security clearances.
Earlier Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters he wasn't sure whether Huang still held a security clearance. He did not offer any specific findings on Huang, and didn't say whether federal investigators interviewed Huang or examined his relationship with an alleged spy.
Blanche said the government relies on a "collective consensus" among federal agencies to assess national security risks and determine whether somebody is able to access sensitive government information.
An Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment on Huang's clearance.
In an interview on CNBC Monday, Mr. Trump broadly defended Huang, saying a "very thorough investigation" found he "did nothing wrong," aside from "bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents."
Asked what Blanche had told him about the situation, Mr. Trump said: "They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he himself was exonerated."
The Justice Department has overseen a criminal investigation into Megaspeed , after the Commerce Department looked into whether Megaspeed had violated export control rules, both agencies confirmed last week. The status of that probe is unclear.
Asked whether the Justice Department investigated Jensen Huang before Mr. Trump assured Nvidia's board that he had not engaged in wrongdoing, Blanche said he would have informed the president if the department had evidence Huang had committed a crime.
"To the extent that that Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this … that's something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true," Blanche said.
Pressed on how the department could rule out potential criminal liability while export-control investigations remained ongoing, Blanche said he could not predict whether future investigations might produce different findings.
"I can't predict the future," Blanche said.
Blanche also described Nvidia as "a good corporate citizen," saying he had no reason to suggest the company was obstructing a federal investigation.
Asked whether Huang's reported relationship with someone allegedly connected to Chinese intelligence presented a national security risk, Blanche said officials must rely on actual intelligence assessments rather than news accounts.
"I don't deal in leaks or in the public reporting that's in some newspaper," Blanche said. "We have to deal with actual facts and what the intelligence community has actually said, which is not something that we should be sharing with the media. And so my personal view of that question is completely irrelevant."

articles.title_orig: Apple Mail added four convenient new features in iOS 27
articles.title_zh: Apple Mail added four convenient new features in iOS 27
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27 brought several new features to the Messages app, including a setting that’s long been a popular request: the ability to customize or turn off the audio button. Here’s how to use it.
With iOS 27, Apple fixed a lot of bugs and also granted many feature requests from over the years.
Siri AI is the biggest example of that, offering a big upgrade over the old Siri. But smaller changes in apps like Calendar , Mail , and Messages reflect this focus on wish fulfillment.
In Messages, there’s a new setting that I instantly starting using. It lets you turn off the audio button that normally lives on the right side of the text input field.
The audio button has been conveniently accessible there for years, but I never use it. I don’t think I’ve ever sent an audio message. Sometimes I use dictation, but that’s always available from the bottom-right of the keyboard.
Since I never need that button, the only time it gets pressed is by accident. And as I suspect a lot of users have encountered— including Justin Bieber —it’s very easy to hit by accident.
Thankfully, iOS 27 has the fix. To disable the audio button, follow these steps:
Even if you turn the audio button off, you can still send audio messages by hitting the + button to open your iMessage apps then selecting ‘Audio.’
If you prefer to keep the button active, you can alternately now select ‘Record Audio’ or ‘Start Dictation’ as its function. That way the button will always stay set to your preference instead of dynamically changing like it did before.
Will you disable the audio button in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Blanche Downplays Questions Over Nvidia as Investigators Examine Company’s Customers
articles.title_zh: Blanche Downplays Questions Over Nvidia as Investigators Examine Company’s Customers
articles.content_orig:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed,  a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .
Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock fell 7% on Tuesday, reversing from a strong 31% rally on Monday, after the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a statement, the board said it had a series of discussions with Huang and was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company. "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain the chair of Nvidia's board.
In an interview on Monday, President Trump said he had spoken "directly and indirectly" with the board and "convinced" them to make a deal. Top administration officials also reportedly assured the Nvidia board that Huang wasn't a national security risk and wasn't facing alleged chip-smuggling charges.
"I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement.
The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees during an hourlong, companywide meeting, stating that his actions were "not acceptable" and violated Nvidia's code of conduct. Huang also said that he was in therapy.
"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang said, per the Times. "I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids, and of course, I hurt all of you."
Huang, however, pushed back against the notion that he was a "tech bro" and above the code of conduct.
He also said his return wasn't the result of the board caving to pressure from President Trump. "That is completely untrue," Huang reportedly said, claiming instead that the board "gathered facts" — including that the DOJ didn't consider him a national security threat — and evaluated whether he deserved a second chance.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, a ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and New York Democrat, called on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify at a public hearing for the House, adding another request for Huang to answer questions on Capitol Hill.
Huang is already scheduled for a transcribed interview with Meeks and the committee chairman, Rep. Brian Mast, next week. Huang is also confirmed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next week.
"Americans deserve answers to the profound questions that are continuing to emerge about NVIDIA and our national security," Meeks wrote. "President Trump's intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as NVIDIA's CEO raises even more concerning questions about the administration's own role, questions the American people deserve to hear answered in public."
President Trump's full-throated support for Jensen Huang and his reinstatement atop Nvidia ( NVDA ) has not been matched by Republican lawmakers, who say they intend to keep the pressure on the chipmaker.
The objections broadly fall into three categories. A handful of Republicans say it was a mistake to reinstate Huang as CEO. Another group says they have serious concerns and feel that US national security has been compromised. And a third group says simply that they have unanswered questions about the whole affair.
According to a Yahoo Finance tally, a majority of the 13 Republican senators whom Huang will face next week on the Senate Banking Committee have offered at least a promise of tough questions, and two members have even said Huang should not be in the CEO chair.
North Dakota Republican Kevin Cramer recently posted that the legal cloud was "risk enough to not rehire Huang," while Nebraska's Pete Ricketts said his "behavior does not support reinstatement." Both will have time to question Huang.
The hearing will be overseen by Chair Tim Scott of South Carolina, who said in his own statement that national security will be "central to the committee's oversight."
Nvidia's board undermined its claims of independence by reinstating CEO Jensen Huang before investigations into his conduct concluded, investors and corporate governance experts said on Monday.
The decision is striking because the board effectively vouched for Huang's candor and fitness to lead the company before its own investigation was complete, raising doubts ‌about whether directors had sufficient information to make an independent judgment, these people said.
Nvidia said on Monday that after talks with senior US officials, its board "is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no ‌national security risk."
… The situation undercuts the board's standing, said New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who helps manage retirement funds that hold some 5 million Nvidia shares.
"They told us flatly that he would not be coming back. They have done a total 180 without any explanation, or any indication that concerns about ‌legal and other liabilities have been resolved," Levine said in a telephone ⁠interview.
"They have proven they're not independent, and that is the defining quality that we need from any board," he said.
Nvidia stock is bouncing off its session lows, but shares remain down over 7% as the chipmaking giant gives back some of its gains made on Monday.
The broader chip sector faced selling pressure as investors rotated out of tech and assessed the implications of Jensen Huang's return as CEO and the market's massive rally the day before.

A Department of Justice official said that President Trump spoke with Attorney General Todd Blanche over the weekend and that the DOJ had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Jensen Huang or Nvidia.
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump stated that Nvidia asked "for assurance on the national security threat."
"And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot," Trump said Monday.
Seaport Research Partners senior analyst Jay Goldberg weighed on Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, telling Yahoo Finance that it was "probably the least bad option for Nvidia."
Still, he noted, "a lot of the issues that I talked about a month ago before we had all of this drama, still exist, right? There are still real questions about their growth prospects and their reliance on some questionable sales to Asia and their their questionable financing deals across the industry. So I certainly still have a lot of questions."

When it comes to the AI trade, this has been the year of AMD ( AMD ). AMD's stock has sizzled, up 112% year to date compared to an 11.5% drop for its top rival Nvidia.
As Nvidia's ( NVDA ) founder Jensen Huang has been embroiled in scandal and the tech trade has been pressured, AMD shares have hung tough. The stock is down 12.2% over the past month versus a 22% decline for Nvidia.
The biggest question for AMD right now is this: Does Huang's stunning return as CEO of Nvidia mean bad news for AMD in 2027 and beyond?
Pros think AMD will be just fine, for now.
"I don't see how this changes it completely," Moor Insights & Strategy founder Patrick Moorhead said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I was saying early on when Jensen left that nothing changes for 18 months. And the reason is the supply chain is locked, the wafers are locked, data center configurations are locked around Nvidia design. So nothing would change, I think, if Jensen had been removed permanently."

articles.title_orig: Shein to pay $100 million to settle federal claims that it deceived U.S. customers
articles.title_zh: Shein to pay $100 million to settle federal claims that it deceived U.S. customers
articles.content_orig:
Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle allegations that the fast-fashion company harmed consumers by misleading them about its products and policies.
The Federal Trade Commission alleges that the Singapore-based retailer made it hard for customers to resolve purchase problems, broke its shipping promises, suppressed negative reviews and engaged in other deceptive practices.
"Shein attracted consumers with promises of affordable clothing, fast delivery and use of suppliers that earned above-average ratings on standards related to child and forced labor, among other representations,"  Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Tuesday. "In reality, the company misled millions of consumers about its products, its suppliers and the authenticity of its customer reviews. Shein further compounded consumer harm by making it extraordinarily difficult to obtain customer service."
Shein, which ships roughly 1 million packages to the U.S. daily, employed only five customer service representatives to field calls from American consumers about their orders, according to the FTC.
Shein also made deceptive claims about its supply chain and the origin of its cotton and failed to provide customers with shipping updates or help them locate late or missing packages, the agency alleged in its complaint .
The $100 million will be used to provide redress to Shein customers, the FTC said. Under the agency's proposed order, Shein is also barred from making misleading claims about shipping and delivery times and from suppressing negative product reviews. The company is also required to provide adequate customer service.
A Shein spokesperson said the agreement "does not constitute an admission of liability, and we continue to disagree with aspects of the FTC's characterization of our business and compliance practices."
Shein went public on the Hong Kong exchange in September. It's built a sizable customer base in the U.S., appealing to shoppers with ultra-cheap clothing styles and fast delivery.
Last year, the White House ended the "de minimis" tariff exemption that allowed low-cost packages, including shipments from Shein, to enter the U.S. duty-free. In April, Shein said it would raise prices for consumers after the loophole closed.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock falls after massive rally, Jensen Huang apologizes to employees
articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock falls after massive rally, Jensen Huang apologizes to employees
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia , and is now tasked with selling the company's artificial intelligence vision while also defending himself in Washington.
As Nvidia employees celebrated the return of their leader to the company's headquarters, Huang told the gathered crowd, "I'll be a better CEO the second time around."
Huang will need to be a better CEO to head off the issues surrounding Nvidia and the broader AI industry exposed by Huang's exit. The challenges include a proliferating roster of investigations and hearings from Congress, regulators and state-level officials , as well as technical and competitive questions about how long Nvidia's currently dominant graphics processing units can remain on top.
"There's nothing prohibiting him from doing what he does on his day job," said Katten chair and former federal prosecutor Gil Soffer. But investigations take significant prep time, Soffer said. "You don't just walk in cold."
At Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, D.C., next week, the company will attempt to convince customers, partners and suppliers that it is developing the future of AI. At the same time, lawmakers will be pressing its newly reinstated CEO over what he knew and when about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang .
Huang, before his scandals, was scheduled to give the GTC DC keynote speech on Dec. 1 to discuss new Nvidia products and the trajectory of the AI ecosystem. In the past, the two-hour speech was the highlight of the event with hordes of fans full of the Huang-inspired "Jensanity."
"People will want to see that it's business as usual, which hopefully for Nvidia shareholders will mean that Jensen Huang announces some new exciting products," said Babson College associate professor Peter Cohan.
Right now, Nvidia has Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, filling the slot. A representative for Nvidia declined to answer multiple questions about whether Huang would appear at the company's event.
On the same day, Huang is scheduled to speak with three House committees — Foreign Affairs, Select Committee on the CCP, and the Select Committee on Intelligence — behind closed doors, where his interview will be transcribed.
"The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the chairs said in a joint statement. They said that Huang has confirmed he will appear for the transcribed interview on Dec. 1.
Next Tuesday's interviews are just the first of a slew of investigations.
On Dec. 3, just as Nvidia's conference is wrapping up, the Senate Banking Committee will hold a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, said Huang will publicly testify as the sole witness.
California's attorney general is also investigating Huang's remarks, and politicians from the Senate Finance, Intelligence, and Foreign Relations committees have inquired about the scandal. In the House, Energy and Commerce has requested a company briefing from Nvidia, in addition to the three committees mentioned earlier. That's not counting an investigation from the Department of Justice and a reported investigation from the Securities and Exchange Commission .
Plus, Huang still has to cooperate with an investigation from the board of directors, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton.
Meanwhile, Nvidia needs Huang to reassure investors and the broader AI ecosystem that the company is developing new products that will be in high demand. Investors had said that while Nvidia's products for the next two years have been fully designed, they were worried that the chipmaker's pace of innovation would slow without Huang.
Nvidia is facing new competition from chips from its biggest customers, including OpenAI , Anthropic , Google , Amazon and Microsoft . The companies have been developing their own chips to reduce reliance on Nvidia, as well as to control AI costs.
"There was already this worry that we're spending too much on it," said Stephanie Balaouras, vice president of group research at Forrester. "One of those cost management strategies is to match ... the workload requirements to the right infrastructure. You don't need to put everything on a Nvidia GPU."
Many in the AI industry see Huang as one of the staunchest defenders of "open-source" AI that is free to use for commercial purposes, as compared with "frontier models" from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which charge users by the token.
Nvidia has also been spending heavily to develop its own open-source models called Nemotron. Currently, Nvidia Vice President Kari Briski is scheduled to present new Nemotron technology at GTC.
On Monday, Nvidia's board said that "senior levels" of the U.S. government provided input on Huang's potential national security risk. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he was central to convincing Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and said he gave the board assurances.
Trump's help could draw even more scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who were already focused on probing Nvidia's chip sales.
"Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy," said Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in a call with reporters Monday.
Republicans have also criticized Huang's return as the focus on the company's China sales intensifies. Still, the investigations could start to weigh on Nvidia's CEO, experts say.
"How could he possibly do the job?" Jeff Sonnenfeld , senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management, told CNBC, citing Senate investigations, House investigations and other state investigations, even before Democrats take over next year.
And the reaction in Washington to Huang's scandal could start to affect Nvidia's sales.
Last week, the Department of Commerce announced that it will prevent Chinese companies from getting around export controls by renting Nvidia's chips across borders. On Monday, Commerce also added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist.
And it's not just Nvidia that is relying on a strong performance from Huang. The company's investors, customers, partners and shareholders will also look to see if Nvidia still wants to be at the center of the AI ecosystem. Before Huang was removed, he pushed Nvidia to invest in AI startups, while selling them products, and helping finance their infrastructure.
Remarks from Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress last week while she was interim CEO suggested that Nvidia would be taking a "very strong look" at using its balance sheet to support the AI ecosystem, but it's unclear if Huang's second stint as CEO will continue with his prior showmanship or abide by a more measured approach.

articles.title_orig: Beverly Hills plastic surgeon branded ‘magician’ over dramatic transformation of 61-year-old mom after $45K facelift
articles.title_zh: Beverly Hills plastic surgeon branded ‘magician’ over dramatic transformation of 61-year-old mom after $45K facelift
articles.content_orig:
Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
But it seems that everyone was blown away by one woman’s recent facelift transformation .
Dr. Marc Levin, a facial plastic surgeon in Beverly Hills , specializes in “dramatic yet undetectable facial rejuvenation.”
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
The expert, 30, who became one of the youngest board-certified surgeons in North America, regularly shares images of his patients before and after their procedures.
Most recently, he uploaded snapshots of 61-year-old hairdresser Helen, who underwent a grueling nine-and-a-half-hour surgery — and the results left the internet stunned.
Dr. Levin shared in the caption of the post: “What a transformation! Absolutely no stone was left unturned for Helen. Every millimeter of her face was analyzed and appropriately addressed.”
He explained how her “character and beauty still remain,” adding: “She is just a younger-looking, more refreshed and clean version of herself.”
Speaking to the California Post, Dr. Levin dished further details about Helen’s “comprehensive facial rejuvenation plan,” which came with a $45,000 price tag.
The extensive list of procedures included an extended deep-plane face and neck lift, endoscopic brow lift, upper blepharoplasty, scarless lower blepharoplasty, facial fat grafting, CO2 laser and an earlobe reduction.
“I’m kind of a younger surgeon so I’m doing the most modern innovations, facial rejuvenation techniques and facelifting techniques,” he told The Post.
And his craftsmanship did not go unnoticed by social media users who flooded to the comments to offer praise.
“Absolutely beautiful… you are so talented and skilled,” one wrote, as another added: “Well, dang…that is a fabulous result!”
Others were quick to brand the surgeon a “magician” and “miracle worker” after seeing the finished results.
In a separate video, Helen, who is originally from South Africa, offered insight on how the procedure had changed her entire outlook.
She began by explaining that she had been “miserable” before taking the plunge to get surgery.
“I looked at the outside of myself and I thought, ‘Oh my God, what is happening to me over here?’ It didn’t match how I was feeling on the inside,” the mom said.
But now, three months post-surgery, she has found a new lease of life.
“I feel like I look like my daughter [now],” Helen revealed, adding: “Thank you for giving me the gift of confidence back.
“How fortunate am I to have the best and most caring surgeon. I’m just so grateful,” she concluded.
Dr. Levin explained that patients will start to see settled results within two to three weeks after surgery.
During this short time frame, “you are able to go out and nobody should know that you had surgery if you have your hair down and makeup on.”
He shared that patients would see their “final results” within three to four months, but will “continuously look better and better for 10 to 12 months after surgery.”

articles.title_orig: GTA VI PC recompilation project shut down by Take-Two
articles.title_zh: GTA VI PC recompilation project shut down by Take-Two
articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
Unsurprisingly, Rockstar Games’ parent, Take-Two Interactive, is trying to stop unauthorized efforts to port Grand Theft Auto 6 to PCs.
One of the most visible community projects to port the game, dubbed Leonida, abruptly shut down on Monday on the software code-hosting platform GitHub, and it turns out Take-Two played a role. GitHub published a Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) notice from Take-Two, which sought the removal of Leonida. GitHub says it “processed the takedown notice against the entire network of 3,007 repositories” that hosted “forked” copies of Leonida’s code.
The DMCA notice came from Take-Two’s “IP Enforcement Team” and flagged Leonida for copyright infringement. The project was among the growing number of community efforts harnessing the leaked Xbox build of GTA 6 from the CyberLeek hacking gang. On Monday, the group dumped a crucial executable for the Xbox build, sparking a scramble among modders to make GTA 6 runnable on PC.
The notable part is how Take-Two justifies the infringement. The developers of Leonida tried to avoid being held responsible for any piracy by not supplying the leaked Xbox files. Take-Two even noted, “The instruction to ‘bring your own files’ attempts to shift the responsibility for supplying files to the user and to make it seem as if this is a general-purpose project.”
However, the company concluded: “This is intentionally misleading — the timing of the project and its explicit focus on Grand Theft Auto establish that the ‘files’ the user must provide are the unauthorized GTA VI files (Take-Two’s IP) in open distribution, and that the developers of the project are aware of this fact. We adamantly request that GitHub disable the repositories and all associated forks from the platform.”
Take-Two also appears to have filed a DMCA takedown notice against Leonida's Discord chat server, according to the project's admin. “Rockstar taking my server down was only part of the reason. Like I’ve said before, I’m a 15-year-old kid. Managing school and sports is hard enough without having middle-aged men yell and complain to you on Discord. Goodbye,” the admin wrote on why he called it quits.
The DMCA filings also suggest Take-Two could go after the growing number of community efforts to port GTA 6 to PC, which are circulating through other GitHub pages and Discord servers. Some of those efforts have been successful at running the opening scenes of the game, although with degraded graphics and low frame rates.
Take-Two didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. But there's been growing speculation about whether the company might rush an official PC release of the game, which has been rumored for Q1 . In the meantime, we’ve seen chatter from modders suggesting they’ll keep their efforts secret to avoid facing legal penalties.
I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector.
Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service.
I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard.
I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

articles.title_orig: Live storm updates: Record king tides leave Bay Area roads flooded
articles.title_zh: Live storm updates: Record king tides leave Bay Area roads flooded
articles.content_orig:
Dangerous high tides, waves reaching up to 30 feet and an incoming storm are expected to bring flooding, heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Northern California this week, threatening coastal communities with road closures, erosion and dangerous beach conditions. The National Weather Service said Tuesday that coastal flooding could reach major to extreme levels in some areas as unusually high tides combine with storm-driven ocean surges.
LIVE: Track rain in San Francisco Bay Area with Live Doppler 7
Low-lying coastal areas could see flooded roads, road closures and erosion. Rising water and waves could also reach farther up beaches than usual, leaving people with fewer ways to escape.
Meanwhile, a cold front is forecast to bring moderate to heavy rain and gusty winds from Tuesday evening into Wednesday morning.
Coastal flood warnings will remain in effect in several areas through Wednesday and Thursday, depending on location.
